correctness.rationale: For adjacent vertices sharing one coordinate, the exact closed-neighborhood symmetric difference comprises the two differing coordinate lines minus their common line. This forces the column-empty/singleton constraints and the lower bound 2l-s, including equality classification for all 3<=s<=l. Every constructed minimum code passes both directions. The unique assigned leaf per row restricts any possible nonadjacent collision to crossed singleton columns, and the collision is present precisely when two rows are untouched by double columns. An inclusion-exclusion count completes the subfamily count. Two exhaustive algorithms agree on all selected-cell subsets for 3x3 to 4x5; a third tests 252000 templates on 5x7. Programs support, but are not used instead of, infinite proof.

originality.rationale: A literature-led distinction is made between local adjacent closed-neighborhood identification, ordinary all-pairs identifying codes, locating-domination and total metric resolution. The prior 2023 foundational paper does not classify the rectangular rook family, and the 2018/2013 rook-graph coding results address different quantifiers. A comparable published rook-graph total-resolving condition reuses row/column structural ideas but does not give the present sharp local minima, exact multiplicity or local-to-global subcount. Novelty remains provisional and conditional on unindexed literature; the scalar global ordinary-identification threshold is not claimed new.
residual_risks: Historical priority is provisional because no finite search can exclude unindexed work and some source variants may not be indexed.

value.rationale: Local identification is an explicitly motivated relaxation of ordinary identifying codes. For the canonical labeled rook graph family, the theorem classifies and exactly counts all optimum local sensor sets, then sharply measures which of them also separate nonadjacent pairs. The ordinary/local mismatch is witnessed already by the 4-by-4 instance, while the counting transition holds for all dimensions. This adds structural and quantitative information absent from old scalar global results, without claiming a paper-sized broader theorem.
